method: chars-per-token, measured against billed output tokens
note: Characters per token, per language. tiktoken is an OpenAI tokenizer and is wrong for Claude, so this file holds measured ratios instead. The factors in `measured` are measured on 15,354 real Claude Code responses that one language dominates, out of 28,678 usable ones on a single machine: an assistant response is written to the transcript as one entry per content block, so reassembling the blocks that share a message.id recovers exactly the characters that its output_tokens paid for. Two disjoint subsets agree to within 1% (2.10 and 2.11 chars per token overall), and responses whose thinking text the transcript did not keep are excluded rather than averaged in. Ubiquitous JSON tool-call scaffolding is measured first and subtracted, because fitting every language at once collapses on its collinearity. A language absent from `measured` carries the hand-set prior scaled by 0.784, the mean ratio of measured to prior across the ten languages that had both: a shape, not a measurement. Run releve-repo.py --calibrate to replace this table with your own machine's, or --tokenizer api for an exact count.
error_bar_note: Median absolute percentage error of 20.7% predicting a whole response from this table, over 28,698 responses (p25 12.3%, p75 28.4%, p90 45.6%). What is not verified is the absolute level: every factor here is measured against output tokens, so a bias common to all of them would not show up in their agreement. Settle it with --tokenizer api, which counts exactly.
default_note: The volume-weighted aggregate across every measured language. Used for an extension this file does not know. Measured languages land between 2.31 and 3.73, so the cost of not knowing one is small next to the cost of the mix.

measured_source.method: output_tokens of one response against the characters of its own content blocks, reassembled across the entries that share its message.id
measured_source.corroboration: markdown (2.99) and the assistant's own natural-language text (2.94) were measured on disjoint sets of responses and agree to within 2%, which is the check that the method is sound rather than fitting noise.
measured_source.wide_spread: typescript (3.73) rests on 260 responses with an interquartile range of 2.39 to 5.86, far wider than any other language here. Treat a TypeScript-heavy count as the loosest number this table produces.
